## Learning Objectives

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Today we will talk about matrix diagonalization.

<br>

We will learn how to __diagonalize__ a square matrix, determine when this is even possible, and interpret it geometrically as a change of basis.

<br>

In addition, we will study the special properties that arise when diagonalizing a __symmetric__ matrix.
:::

## Diagonalization

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Given a _square_ matrix $A$, our goal for today is to find a factorization of $A$ is of the form 

$$
A = PDP^{-1}
$$

where:

- $D$ and $P$ are square matrices of the same size as $A$,
- $P$ is invertible (so that $P^{-1}$ exists), and
- $D$ is a __diagonal__ matrix, meaning that it only has non-zero entries on the diagonal. (In other words, it is both an upper triangular and lower triangular matrix at the same time.)
:::

## Diagonalization

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
Recall from last week that two $n \times n$ matrices $A$ and $B$ are said to be __similar__ if there is an invertible matrix $P$ such that $P^{-1}AP = B,$ or, equivalently, $A = PBP^{-1}$.

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        A square matrix $A$ is said to be <b>diagonalizable</b> if \(A\) is similar to a diagonal matrix.
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

<br> 

That is, if we can find some invertible $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}
$$ 

and $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

<br>

This factorization $A = PDP^{-1}$ allows us to represent $A$ in a form that exposes many interesting properties of $A$.

Let's start by showing one benefit of this factorization: we can compute $A^k$ quickly for large values of $k$.
:::

## Powers of a Diagonal Matrix

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
As a starting point, let's see how simple it is to take powers of a _diagonal_ matrix.

<br>

__Example.__ Consider taking the powers of the following diagonal matrix

$$
D = \begin{bmatrix}5&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}.
$$ 

Note that $D^2 = \begin{bmatrix}5&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}5^2&0\\0&3^2\end{bmatrix},$ and <tab>$D^3 = DD^2 = \begin{bmatrix}5&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5^2&0\\0&3^2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}5^3&0\\0&3^3\end{bmatrix}.$

<br>

So in general,

$$
D^k = \begin{bmatrix}5^k&0\\0&3^k\end{bmatrix} \;\;\;\mbox{for}\;k\geq1.
$$
:::

## Extending to a General Matrix

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}

Now, let's extend this idea to apply also to any __diagonalizable__ matrix $A$.

Once again, let's see this by example.

 __Example.__ Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}7&2\\-4&1\end{bmatrix}.$ Find a formula for $A^k$. Use the fact that

$$
A = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\-1&-2\end{bmatrix}}_{P} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}5&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}}_{D} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&-1\end{bmatrix}}_{P^{-1}},
$$

which we show below using `Python`

```{python}
import numpy as np
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
P = np.array([[ 1,  1],
              [-1, -2]])
D = np.array([[ 5,  0],
              [ 0,  3]])
Pinv = np.array([[ 2,  1],
                 [-1, -1]])
assert(np.allclose(Pinv, np.linalg.inv(P))) # check that P and Pinv are inverses
print(P @ D @ Pinv)                         # calculate A = P D P^{-1}
```
:::

## Extending to a General Matrix

:::{style="font-size: .5em"}
__Solution.__  By associativity of matrix multiplication,

$$
\begin{align*}
A^2 &= (PDP^{-1})(PDP^{-1}) \\
&= PD(P^{-1}P)DP^{-1} \\
&= PDDP^{-1} \\
&= PD^2P^{-1}
\end{align*}
$$

$$
= \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\-1&-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5^2&0\\0&3^2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&-1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The same pattern occurs for $A^3$, $A^4$, and so on. In general, for $k\geq 1,$

$$
A^k = PD^kP^{-1}.
$$

For this particular matrix $A$, we find that

$$
\begin{align*}
A^k &= P D^k P^{-1} \\
&=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\-1&-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5^k&0\\0&3^k\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&-1\end{bmatrix} \\
&=\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot5^k-3^k&5^k-3^k\\2\cdot3^k-2\cdot5^k&2\cdot3^k-5^k\end{bmatrix}.
\end{align*}
$$
:::

## The Need for Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues{.really-really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.2em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        <span class="label">
        The Diagonalization Theorum</span>
        An \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\) is diagonalizable if and only if \(A\) has \(n\) <b>linearly independent</b> eigenvectors.
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

<br>

In other words, $A$ is diagonalizable if and only if there are enough eigenvectors to form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$.  
 
 <br>

We call such a basis an __eigenvector basis__ or an __eigenbasis__ of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
:::

## The Need for Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues{.really-really-smaller-title}

In fact, if there are $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors, then we can write $A = PDP^{-1}$ where:

- The columns of $P$ are the $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors of $A$.
- The __diagonal entries of $D$ are eigenvalues__ of $A$ that correspond, respectively, to the eigenvectors in $P$.

<br>

__Example.__ A $2 \times 2$ rotation matrix like

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & -1 \\
1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
$$

is not diagonalizable, because we saw last week that it does not have any (real-valued) eigenvalues.

## The Need for Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues{.really-really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.2em"}
__Proof ($\Rightarrow$ direction).__

> If $A$ is diagonalizable, then it has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors.

<br>

In this direction, we are given a matrix $A$ that is assumed to be diagonalizable, so it is possible to write $A$ in the form $A = PDP^{-1}$. If we right-multiply both sides of this equation by $P$, we find that

$$
AP = PD.
$$

<br>

Also, it is given that $P$ is invertible, which means that its columns must be linearly independent (by the Invertible Matrix Theorem).
:::

## The Need for Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues{.really-really-smaller-title}

Observe that if $P$ is any $n\times n$ matrix with columns $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_n,$ then

$$
AP = A[\mathbf{v}_1\;\mathbf{v}_2\;\cdots\;\mathbf{v}_n] = [A\mathbf{v}_1\;A\mathbf{v}_2\;\cdots\;A\mathbf{v}_n]
$$

<br>

Next, note if $D$ is any diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n,$ then

$$
PD =
\begin{bmatrix}| & | & & | \\{\bf v}_1 &{\bf v}_2 & \cdots &{\bf v}_n \\ | & | & & | \\ | & |  & & | \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_1&0&\cdots&0\\0&\lambda_2&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&\lambda_n\end{bmatrix}
= [\lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1\;\lambda_2\mathbf{v}_2\;\cdots\;\lambda_n\mathbf{v}_n].
$$

<br>

Since we are given that $AP = PD$, the calculations above show that

$$
[A\mathbf{v}_1\;A\mathbf{v}_2\;\cdots\;A\mathbf{v}_n] = [\lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1\;\lambda_2\mathbf{v}_2\;\cdots\;\lambda_n\mathbf{v}_n].
$$

## The Need for Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues{.really-really-smaller-title}

Equating columns, we find that

$$
A\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1, \;\;\; A\mathbf{v}_2 = \lambda_2\mathbf{v}_2, \;\;\; \dots, \;\;\; A\mathbf{v}_n = \lambda_n\mathbf{v}_n.
$$

Because $A{\bf v_i}$ is scaling ${\bf v_i}$ by $\lambda_i$, we know ${\bf v_i}$ must be an eigenvector of $A$ and $\lambda_i$ must be its corresponding eigenvalue.

<br>

Hence, the columns of $P$ are eigenvectors of $A$. Additionally, we already showed that the columns of $P$ are linearly independent by the IMT.

<br>

Therefore: if $A$ is diagonalizable, then it has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors.

## The Need for Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues{.really-really-smaller-title}

__Proof ($\Leftarrow$ direction).__

> If $A$ has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors, then $A$ is diagonalizable.

Using the ideas from the first half of the proof, we now see how to _construct_ the diagonalization of $A$.

- Let $P$ be a matrix whose columns are the $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors of $A$.
- Let $D$ be a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the corresponding eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$.

Using the sequence of equations from earlier in reverse order, we can go from 

$$
A\mathbf{v}_1 = \lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1, \;\;\; A\mathbf{v}_2 = \lambda_2\mathbf{v}_2, \;\;\; \dots, \;\;\; A\mathbf{v}_n = \lambda_n\mathbf{v}_n
$$

to 

$$
AP = PD.
$$

Since the eigenvectors are given as linearly independent, $P$ is invertible (by the IMT) and so 

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

## The Need for Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues{.really-really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.2em"}
The takeaway is this:

<br>

Every $n\times n$ matrix having $n$ **linearly independent** eigenvectors can be factored into the product of 

* a matrix $P$, 
* a diagonal matrix $D$, and
* the inverse of $P$ 

... where $P$ holds the eigenvectors of $A$, and $D$ holds the eigenvalues of $A$.

<br>

This is the __eigendecomposition__ of $A$. It is quite fundamental!
:::


## How to Diagonalize

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Let's put this all together and show a four-step procedure to diagonalize a matrix: find eigenvalues, find eigenvectors, construct $P$, and construct $D$.

<br>

__Example.__  Diagonalize the following matrix, if possible.

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}1&3&3\\-3&-5&-3\\3&3&1\end{bmatrix}
$$

<br>

That is, find an invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $A = PDP^{-1}.$
:::

## 1: Find the eigenvalues
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
In this case, the characteristic equation turns out to involve a cubic polynomial that can be factored:

$$
\begin{align*}
0 &= \det(A-\lambda I) \\
&= \det\left( \begin{bmatrix}1 - \lambda &3&3\\-3&-5 - \lambda &-3\\3&3&1 - \lambda\end{bmatrix} \right) \\
&= -\lambda^3 - 3\lambda^2 + 4 \\
&= -(\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)^2.
\end{align*}
$$

<br>

So the eigenvalues are $\lambda = 1$ and $\lambda = -2$ (with algebraic multiplicity two).
:::

## 2: Find $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors{.really-really-smaller-title}

_This is the step where we find out whether or not $A$ can be diagonalized._ The answer depends on whether we can form $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors.

<br>

In this example, we need _three_ linearly independent vectors because $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix.

Using our standard method (finding the nullspace of $A - \lambda I$) we find a basis for each eigenspace:

Basis for $\lambda = 1$:

- We must find the nullspace of
$A - I = \begin{bmatrix}1-1&3&3\\-3&-5-1&-3\\3&3&1-1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&3&3\\-3&-6&-3\\3&3&0\end{bmatrix}$.

- Note that this matrix has rank 2 so it has a nullspace of dimension 1.

- Using Gauss-Jordan elimination, we can find a nonzero solution to the homogeneous equation $(A - I) {\bf v} = 0$, namely $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{bmatrix}.$

## 2: Find $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors{.really-really-smaller-title}

Using the same technique, we can find the basis for $\lambda = -2$. It turns out that the result is:

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix} \;\text{ and }\; \mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

At this point we must ensure that $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ forms a linearly independent set.

<br>

These particular vectors in fact do. There are many ways to check this: 

- you can use solve the homogeneous vector equation $c_1 {\bf v}_1 + c_2 {\bf v}_2 + c_3 {\bf v}_3 = {\bf 0}$ using Gauss-Jordan elimination, 

- or you can apply any part of the Invertible Matrix Theorem.

## 3: Construct $P$ from the Eigenvectors{.really-smaller-title}

The order of the vectors is actually not important (yet).

<br>

:::{style="font-size: 1.5em"}
$$
P = [\mathbf{v}_1\;\mathbf{v}_2\;\mathbf{v}_3] = \begin{bmatrix}1&-1&-1\\-1&1&0\\1&0&1\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:::

## 4: Construct $D$ with Corresponding Eigenvalues{.really-really-smaller-title}

The order of eigenvalues must match the order of eigenvectors used in the previous step.

<br>

If an eigenvalue has multiplicity greater than 1, then repeat it the corresponding number of times.

$$
D = \begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&-2&0\\0&0&-2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

<br>

And we are done.   We have diagonalized $A$:

$$
A =  \begin{bmatrix}1&3&3\\-3&-5&-3\\3&3&1\end{bmatrix} =
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&-1\\-1&1&0\\1&0&1\end{bmatrix}}_{P} \:
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&-2&0\\0&0&-2\end{bmatrix}}_{D} \:
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&-1\\-1&1&0\\1&0&1\end{bmatrix}^{-1}}_{P^{-1}}
$$

## 4: Construct $D$ with Corresponding Eigenvalues{.really-really-smaller-title}

We can check our work using Python.

:::{style="font-size: 1.2em"}
```{python}
#| echo: true
P = np.array([[ 1, -1, -1],
              [-1,  1,  0],
              [ 1,  0,  1]])
D = np.array([[ 1,  0,  0],
              [ 0, -2,  0],
              [ 0,  0, -2]])
print(P @ D @ np.linalg.inv(P))
```
:::

<br>

So, just as a reminder, we can now take powers of $A$ quite efficiently:

$$
A^{100} = \begin{bmatrix}1&-1&-1\\-1&1&0\\1&0&1\end{bmatrix}  \begin{bmatrix}1^{100}&0&0\\0&(-2)^{100}&0\\0&0&(-2)^{100}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&-1\\-1&1&0\\1&0&1\end{bmatrix}^{-1}
$$

## When Diagonalization Fails

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}

Let's look at another example, this time for a matrix that turns out not to be diagonalizable.

__Example.__ Diagonalize the following matrix, if possible.

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}2&4&3\\-4&-6&-3\\3&3&1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

<br>

__Solution.__ Let's follow our 4-step procedure.

In step 1, we calculate the eigenvalues of $A$. The characteristic equation of $A$ turns out to be the same as in the last example:

$$
0 = \det(A-\lambda I) = -(\lambda-1)(\lambda +2)^2.
$$

So, the eigenvalues are $\lambda = 1$ with multiplicity one, and $\lambda = -2$ with multiplicity two.
:::

## When Diagonalization Fails

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
In step 2, we calculate the eigenvectors of $A$ by finding the nullspace of $A - \lambda I$.

This time, it turns out that each of the matrices have rank 2.

$$
A - I = \begin{bmatrix}1&4&3\\-4&-7&-3\\3&3&0\end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad A + 2I = \begin{bmatrix}4&4&3\\-4&-4&-3\\3&5&1\end{bmatrix}
$$

<br>

As a result, each eigenspace is only one-dimensional:

Basis for $\lambda_1 = 1$: $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{bmatrix}.$ Hence, the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda_1$ is 1.

Basis for $\lambda_2 = -2$: $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}.$ Hence, the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda_2$ is 1 as well.
:::

## When Diagonalization Fails

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

There are no other eigenvalues, and every eigenvector of $A$ is a multiple of either $\mathbf{v}_1$ or $\mathbf{v}_2.$  

<br>

Hence, it is impossible to construct $n = 3$ linearly independent eigenvectors of $A$. 

So we conclude that $A$ is __not__ diagonalizable.

<br>

In general, to be diagonalizable, the algebraic multiplicity of each eigenvalue has to be equal to its geometric multiplicity.
:::

## A Special Case

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}

There is an important situation in which we can conclude immediately that $A$ is diagonalizable, without explicitly constructing and testing the eigenspaces of $A$.

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        An \(n\times n\) matrix with $n$ distinct eigenvalues has \(n\) linearly independent eigenvectors, and therefore is diagonalizable.
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

<br>

__Example.__ Determine if the following matrix is diagonalizable.

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}5&-8&1\\0&0&7\\0&0&-2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

__Solution.__

- Since $A$ is (upper) triangular, its eigenvalues are $5, 0,$ and $-2$.
- Since $A$ is a $3\times3$ with 3 distinct eigenvalues, $A$ is diagonalizable.
:::

## Diagonalization as Change of Basis{.smaller-title}


We can now turn to a __geometric__ understanding of how diagonalization informs us about the properties of $A$.

<br>

Let's interpret the diagonalization $A = PDP^{-1}$ in terms of how $A$ acts as a linear operator.

<br>

In doing so, diagonalization has a specific interpretation: 

> Diagonalization separates the influence of each vector component from the others.

## Diagonalization as Change of Basis{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
To see what this means, let's first consider an easier case: a diagonal matrix. When we multiply a vector $\mathbf{x}$ by a diagonal matrix $D$, the change to each component of $\mathbf{x}$ depends only on that component.

That is, multiplying by a diagonal matrix simply __scales__ the components of the vector.

<br>

__Example.__ Let $D = \begin{bmatrix}5&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}.$ Then, $D \begin{bmatrix}x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}5x_1 \\ 3x_2 \end{bmatrix}.$

<br>

On the other hand, when we multiply by a matrix $A$ that has off-diagonal entries, the components of $\mathbf{x}$ affect each other.

So diagonalizing a matrix allows us to bring intuition to its behavior as as linear operator.
:::

## Geometrically Interpreting Diagonalization{.really-really-smaller-title}


:::{style="font-size: 1.2em"}
Because $P$ is square and invertible, its columns form a basis for $\mathbb{R}^n$.  Let's call that basis $\mathcal{B} = \{\mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2, \dots, \mathbf{p}_n\}.$  

Now let's think about matrix-vector multiplication as a change of basis -- that is, moving between the standard basis and the $\mathcal{B}$ basis.

<br>

Recall from Week 7 that if we have a vector ${\bf y}$ in the standard basis and we want to find its coordinates in the basis $\mathcal{B}$, then we can to solve the system of equations

$$\mathbf{y} = P\mathbf{x} = x_1 {\bf p}_1 + x_2 {\bf p}_2 + \cdots + x_n {\bf p}_n$$

to find a vector ${\bf x}$ such that ${\bf x} = [{\bf y}]_{\mathcal{B}}$.

<br>

:::

## Geometrically Interpreting Diagonalization{.really-really-smaller-title}


:::{style="font-size: 1.2em"}
Since $P$ is invertible, we can use its inverse to solve this system of equations and find that ${\bf x} = P^{-1} {\bf y}$.

Similarly, if we start with a vector ${\bf x}$ in the $\mathcal{B}$-basis and want to calculate its coordinates in the standard basis, we can compute ${\bf y} = P {\bf x}$.

That is: ${\bf y}$ is the point (in the standard basis) that has coordinates ${\bf x}$ in the basis $\mathcal{B}$.

:::

## Geometrically Interpreting Diagonalization{.really-really-smaller-title}

So we can interpret $A {\bf x} = PDP^{-1}\mathbf{x}$ as the following three step geometric transformation:

_Step 1._ Compute the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ in the basis $\mathcal{B}$.   

This is $P^{-1}\mathbf{x}.$

<br>

_Step 2._ Scale those coordinates according to the diagonal matrix $D$.   
This is $DP^{-1}\mathbf{x}.$ (Remember that composition of matrices goes from right to left!)

<br>

_Step 3._ Find the point in the standad basis that has those scaled coordinates in the basis $\mathcal{B}.$ 

This is $PDP^{-1}\mathbf{x}.$

```{python}
#| echo: true
A = np.array([[ 1.86363636, 0.68181819],
              [-0.22727273, 3.13636364]])

P = np.array([[0.98058068, 0.51449576],
              [0.19611614, 0.85749293]])
D = np.array([[2, 0],
              [0, 3]])

np.allclose(A, P @ D @ np.linalg.inv(P))
```


## Geometrically Interpreting Diagonalization{.really-really-smaller-title}

__Example.__ Let's visualize diagonalization geometrically.

Consider a fixed-but-unwritten matrix $A$. Below shows how it transforms a point $\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}2.47\\1.25\end{bmatrix}$.

```{python}
import laUtilities as ut

ax = ut.plotSetup(-1,6,-1,6,size=(12,5))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
v1 = np.array([5.0,1.0])
v1 = v1 / np.sqrt(np.sum(v1*v1))
v2 = np.array([3.0,5.0])
v2 = v2 / np.sqrt(np.sum(v2*v2))
p1 = 2*v1+v2
p2 = 4*v1+3*v2
ut.plotVec(ax, p1,'k')
ut.plotVec(ax, p2,'k')
ax.annotate('', xy=(p2[0], p2[1]),  xycoords='data',
                xytext=(p1[0], p1[1]), textcoords='data',
                size=15,
                arrowprops={'arrowstyle': 'simple',
                                'fc': '0.7', 
                                'ec': 'none',
                                'connectionstyle' : 'arc3,rad=-0.3'},
                )
ax.text(2.5,0.75,r'${\bf x}$',size=20)
ax.text(5.2,2.75,r'$A{\bf x}$',size=20)
ax.plot(0,0,'');
```

So far, we cannot say much about what the linear transformation $A$ does in general.

## Geometrically Interpreting Diagonalization{.really-really-smaller-title}

Now, let's compute $P^{-1}\mathbf{x}.$ Remember that the columns of $P$ are the eigenvectors of $A$.

So $P^{-1}\mathbf{x}$ is the coordinates of the point $\mathbf{x}$ in the __eigenvector basis__:

```{python}
#
ax = ut.plotSetup(-1,6,-1,6,size=(12,5))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
v1 = np.array([5.0,1.0])
v1 = v1 / np.sqrt(np.sum(v1*v1))
v2 = np.array([3.0,5.0])
v2 = v2 / np.sqrt(np.sum(v2*v2))
ut.plotVec(ax,v1,'b')
ut.plotVec(ax,v2)
ut.plotLinEqn(-v1[1],v1[0],0,color='b')
ut.plotLinEqn(-v2[1],v2[0],0,color='r')
for i in range(-4,8):
    ut.plotLinEqn(-v1[1],v1[0],i*(v1[0]*v2[1]-v1[1]*v2[0]),format=':',color='b')
    ut.plotLinEqn(-v2[1],v2[0],i*(v2[0]*v1[1]-v2[1]*v1[0]),format=':',color='r')
p1 = 2*v1+v2
p2 = 4*v1+3*v2
ut.plotVec(ax, p1,'k')
ax.text(2.5,0.75,r'${\bf x}$',size=20)
ax.text(v2[0]-0.15,v2[1]+0.5,r'${\bf p_2}$',size=20)
ax.text(v1[0]-0.15,v1[1]+0.35,r'${\bf p_1}$',size=20)
ax.plot(0,0,'');
```

The coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ in this basis are (2,1). In other words $P^{-1}\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}.$

## Geometrically Interpreting Diagonalization{.really-really-smaller-title}

Now, we compute $DP^{-1}\mathbf{x}.$  Since $D$ is diagonal, this is just scaling each of the $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates.  

In this example the eigenvalue corresponding to $\mathbf{p}_1$ is 2, and the eigenvalue corresponding to $\mathbf{p}_2$ is 3.

```{python}
#
ax = ut.plotSetup(-1,6,-1,6,size=(12,4))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
v1 = np.array([5.0,1.0])
v1 = v1 / np.sqrt(np.sum(v1*v1))
v2 = np.array([3.0,5.0])
v2 = v2 / np.sqrt(np.sum(v2*v2))
#ut.plotVec(ax,v1,'b')
#ut.plotVec(ax,v2)
ut.plotLinEqn(-v1[1],v1[0],0,color='b')
ut.plotLinEqn(-v2[1],v2[0],0,color='r')
for i in range(-4,8):
    ut.plotLinEqn(-v1[1],v1[0],i*(v1[0]*v2[1]-v1[1]*v2[0]),format=':',color='b')
    ut.plotLinEqn(-v2[1],v2[0],i*(v2[0]*v1[1]-v2[1]*v1[0]),format=':',color='r')
p1 = 2*v1+v2
p2 = 4*v1+3*v2
ut.plotVec(ax, p1,'k')
ut.plotVec(ax, p2,'k')
ax.annotate('', xy=(p2[0], p2[1]),  xycoords='data',
                xytext=(p1[0], p1[1]), textcoords='data',
                size=15,
                #bbox=dict(boxstyle="round", fc="0.8"),
                arrowprops={'arrowstyle': 'simple',
                                'fc': '0.7', 
                                'ec': 'none',
                                'connectionstyle' : 'arc3,rad=-0.3'},
                )
ax.text(2.5,0.75,r'${\bf x}$',size=20)
ax.text(5.2,2.75,r'$A{\bf x}$',size=20)
ax.plot(0,0,'');
```

So the coordinates of $A\mathbf{x}$ in the basis $\mathcal{B}$ are 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

## Geometrically Interpreting Diagonalization{.really-really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .9em"}
Now we convert back to the standard basis -- that is, we ask which point has coordinates (4,3) in basis $\mathcal{B}.$


We rely on the fact that if $\mathbf{y}$ has coordinates $\mathbf{x}$ in the basis $\mathcal{B}$, then $\mathbf{y} = P\mathbf{x}.$ So $A\mathbf{x} = P\begin{bmatrix}4\\3\end{bmatrix} = PDP^{-1}\mathbf{x}.$

## Geometrically Interpreting Diagonalization{.really-really-smaller-title}

In conclusion: notice that the transformation $\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ may be a complicated one in which each component of $\mathbf{x}$ affects each component of $A\mathbf{x}$.   

However, by changing to the basis defined by the eigenspaces of $A$, the action of $A$ becomes simple to understand. 

<br>

Diagonalization of $A$ __changes to a basis in which the action of $A$ is particularly easy to understand and compute with.__

<br>

Remember that not all matrices are diagonalizable! This particular matrix factorization only applies to square matrices, and not even all square matrices.

<br>

Next week, we will design a generalization of diagonalization that does apply to all matrices. It is called __singular value decomposition__, and it is the strongest tool from linear algebra that we have been building up to in this course. We will then explore its data science applications.

## Symmetric Matrices

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        A symmetric matrix is a matrix \(A\) such that \(A^\top = A\).
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

Note that if $A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix, then $A^\top$ is an $n \times m$ matrix. For these to be equal, a symmetric matrix __must__ be square.

<br>

__Example.__ Here are three __symmetric__ matrices:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-3\end{bmatrix},\;\;\;\;\begin{bmatrix}0&-1&0\\-1&5&8\\0&8&-7\end{bmatrix},\;\;\;\;\begin{bmatrix}a&b&c\\b&d&e\\c&e&f\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here are three __nonsymmetric__ matrices:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1&-3\\3&0\end{bmatrix},\;\;\;\;\begin{bmatrix}1&3&0\\3&1&0\end{bmatrix},\;\;\;\;\begin{bmatrix}1&-4&0\\-6&1&-4\\0&-6&1\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

## Symmetric Matrices

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
__Example.__ Another example of a symmetric matrix is $A^\top A$ (starting from _any_ matrix $A$, even a non-square matrix).

Recall that $A^\top A$ is used within the normal equations $A^\top A\mathbf{x} = A^\top \mathbf{b}$ to solve the least-squares problem. Here is an example.

```{python}
#| echo: true
A = np.array([[1, 2, 3],
              [4, 5, 6]])
print(A.T @ A)
```

<br>

Given any matrix $A$, the matrix $A^\top A$ is always symmetric because

$$
(A^\top A)^\top = A^\top (A^\top)^\top = (A^\top A).
$$

In the remainder of this week, we'll see that symmetric matrices have properties that relate to both eigendecomposition and orthogonality.
:::

## Diagonalizing Symmetric Matrices{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Symmetric matrices have a number of interesting properties. For example, the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix are __orthogonal__

__Example.__ Diagonalize the following symmetric matrix:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}6&-2&-1\\-2&6&-1\\-1&-1&5\end{bmatrix}
$$

The characteristic equation of $A$ is

$$\begin{align*}
0 &= \det(A - \lambda I) \\
&= -\lambda^3 + 17\lambda^2 -90\lambda + 144 \\
&= -(\lambda-8)(\lambda-6)(\lambda-3)
\end{align*}
$$

So the eigenvalues are 8, 6, and 3.
:::

## Diagonalizing Symmetric Matrices{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .7em"}
We construct a basis for each eigenspace, using our standard method of finding the nullspace of $A-\lambda I$:

$$
\lambda_1 = 8: \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix};\;\;\;\;\lambda_2=6: \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\-1\\2\end{bmatrix};\;\;\;\;\;\lambda_3=3: \mathbf{v}_3=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

These three vectors form a basis for $\mathbb{R}^3.$

<br>

But here is the remarkable thing: these three vectors form an __orthogonal set.__ That is, any two eigenvectors are orthogonal. 

$$\begin{align*}
\mathbf{v}_1^\top \mathbf{v}_2 &= (-1)(-1) + (1)(-1) + (0)(2) = 0 \\
\mathbf{v}_1^\top \mathbf{v}_3 &= (-1)(1) + (1)(1) + (0)(1) = 0 \\
\mathbf{v}_2^\top \mathbf{v}_3 &= (-1)(1) + (-1)(1) + (2)(1) = 0
\end{align*}
$$

As a result, $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ form an __orthogonal basis__ for $\mathbb{R}^3.$
:::

## Diagonalizing Symmetric Matrices{.smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
Let's normalize these vectors so they each have length 1:

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}-1/\sqrt{2}\\1/\sqrt{2}\\0\end{bmatrix};\;\;\;\;\mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}-1/\sqrt{6}\\-1/\sqrt{6}\\2/\sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix};\;\;\;\;\; \mathbf{u}_3=\begin{bmatrix}1/\sqrt{3}\\1/\sqrt{3}\\1/\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

The orthogonality of the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix is quite important.

<br>

To see this, let's write the diagonalization of $A$ in terms of these eigenvectors and eigenvalues:

$$
P = \begin{bmatrix}-1/\sqrt{2}&-1/\sqrt{6}&1/\sqrt{3}\\1/\sqrt{2}&-1/\sqrt{6}&1/\sqrt{3}\\0&2/\sqrt{6}&1/\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix},\;\;\;\;D = \begin{bmatrix}8&0&0\\0&6&0\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then, $A = PDP^{-1}$ as usual.

<br>

Since $P$ is square and has orthonormal columns, $P$ is an __orthogonal__ matrix (AKA an __orthonormal__ matrix).

That means $P^{-1} = P^\top$ and $A = PDP^\top.$
:::

## The Spectral Theorum

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        If \(A\) is symmetric, then any two eigenvectors of \(A\) from different eigenspaces are orthogonal.
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

__Proof.__ 

Let $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ be eigenvectors that correspond to distinct eigenvalues, say, $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$  

To show that $\mathbf{v}_1^\top \mathbf{v}_2 = 0,$ compute

$$
\begin{align*}
\lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1^\top \mathbf{v}_2 &= (\lambda_1\mathbf{v}_1)^\top \mathbf{v}_2 \\
&=(A\mathbf{v}_1)^\top \mathbf{v}_2 \\
&=(\mathbf{v}_1^\top A^\top )\mathbf{v}_2 \\
&=\mathbf{v}_1^\top (A^\top \mathbf{v}_2) \\
&=\mathbf{v}_1^\top (A\mathbf{v}_2) \quad \gets \text{this is where we use the fact that $A$ is symmetric} \\
&=\mathbf{v}_1^\top (\lambda_2\mathbf{v}_2) \\
&=\lambda_2\mathbf{v}_1^\top \mathbf{v}_2
\end{align*}
$$
:::

## The Spectral Theorum

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

So we conclude that $\lambda_1(\mathbf{v}_1^\top \mathbf{v}_2) = \lambda_2(\mathbf{v}_1^\top \mathbf{v}_2).$

But $\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2,$ so this can only happen if $\mathbf{v}_1^\top \mathbf{v}_2 = 0.$

So $\mathbf{v}_1$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{v}_2.$

<br>

The same argument applies to any other pair of eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues.

So any two eigenvectors of $A$ from different eigenspaces are orthogonal.
:::

## Orthogonal Diagonalization

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
We can now introduce a special kind of diagonalizability:

<br>

An $n\times n$ matrix is said to be __orthogonally diagonalizable__ if there are an orthogonal matrix $P$ (with $P^{-1} = P^\top$) and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that 

$$
A = PDP^\top = PDP^{-1}
$$

<br>

Such a diagonalization requires $n$ linearly independent and __orthonormal__ eigenvectors.

When is this possible?
:::

## Orthogonal Diagonalization

:::{style="font-size: .7em"}
If $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable, then

$$
A^\top  = (PDP^\top )^\top  = (P^\top )^\top D^\top P^\top  = PDP^\top  = A
$$

So $A$ is symmetric!

<br>

It turns out the converse is true.

Hence we obtain the following theorem:

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        An \(n\times n\) matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is a symmetric matrix.
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```
:::
